references.text: The context of the parable: The Lord gave each of his ten servants a mina and said, 'Engage in business with these until I come back' ([ref:Luk 19:13|Luke 19:13]). Verse 16 shows the first servant reporting the result of his faithful stewardship.

In the parable of the talents in [ref:Matt 25:20-21|Matthew 25:20-21], the servant who received five talents and earned five more comes forward, and the master praises him as 'faithful.' The parallel is clear: faithful stewardship of what has been entrusted yields multiplied returns.
The parable of the talents in [ref:Matt 25:14-15|Matthew 25:14-15] is a parallel account where a master entrusts his servants with different amounts, corresponding to the minas in Luke 19.

The Lord's response to the faithful servant in [ref:Luk 19:17|Luke 19:17]: 'Well done, good servant! Because you have been faithful in a very little, you shall have authority over ten cities.' The reward is directly linked to the fruit of the service in verse 16.
[ref:1 Kor 4:2|1 Corinthians 4:2] states that what is required of stewards is faithfulness. The first servant in Luke 19:16 demonstrates this very faithfulness by returning with ten times as much.

[ref:Luk 16:10|Luke 16:10] expresses the principle that whoever is faithful in a very little is also faithful in much. The servant who received one mina and earned ten illustrates this principle in practice.

[ref:Ordsp 22:29|Proverbs 22:29] says that whoever is diligent in their work will stand before kings. The servant who was industrious and multiplied the value of his mina by ten illustrates this wisdom.

In [ref:1 Mos 39:2-4|Genesis 39:2-4], the Lord was with Joseph so that everything he did prospered, and he was entrusted with all. Joseph's faithful service is an Old Testament foreshadowing of the faithful servant who multiplies what has been entrusted to him.
